When the per-feature loss scaling exponent β is less than the feature frequency exponent α, SAEs enter a pathological regime where they learn far fewer features than the number of latents.
Experiments on synthetic manifolds show that the loss scaling curve depends on manifold geometry; some manifolds allow gradual loss reduction with more latents, while others saturate quickly.
Analysis of real SAEs (Gemma Scope and Inception-v1) shows some latents with high cosine similarity, but evidence for pathological tiling is inconclusive.
The presence of radial variation in feature manifolds may cause SAEs to learn basis-like solutions rather than tiling, suggesting pathological scaling might not occur in practice.
papers.limitation:
The assumptions of feature-specific latents, decoder respect for subspaces, and orthogonal feature subspaces may not hold in practice (e.g., due to feature absorption and non-orthogonality).
The model assumes power-law distributions for feature frequencies and loss scaling, which may not accurately reflect real data.
The question of whether SAEs are in the pathological regime is not resolved due to uncertainty about real feature geometries and frequencies.
future_direction: Estimating the feature frequency exponent α and loss scaling exponent β for real SAEs.
Studying the geometry of real feature manifolds to better understand SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) model the activations of a neural network as linear combinations of sparsely occurring directions of variation (latents). The ability of SAEs to reconstruct activations follows scaling laws w.r.t. the number of latents. In this work, we adapt a capacity-allocation model from the neural scaling literature (Brill, 2024) to understand SAE scaling, and in particular, to understand how "feature manifolds" (multi-dimensional features) influence scaling behavior. Consistent with prior work, the model recovers distinct scaling regimes. Notably, in one regime, feature manifolds have the pathological effect of causing SAEs to learn far fewer features in data than there are latents in the SAE. We provide some preliminary discussion on whether or not SAEs are in this pathological regime in the wild.

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
Using language-specific features as gating signals to improve steering vectors achieves better control over the language generated by LLMs, with improved performance and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The method does not yet cover certain low-resource languages.
The SAE-based steering vectors sometimes underperform compared to the original steering vectors.
The SAEs used were not trained on curated multilingual data.
future_direction: Utilize language-specific features to guide the training process of multilingual language models.
Investigate low-resource languages to enhance the analysis.
Explore more refined approaches to improve the performance of SAE-based steering vectors.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms behind multilingual capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been examined using neuron-based or internal-activation-based methods. However, these methods often face challenges such as superposition and layer-wise activation variance, which limit their reliability. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer a more nuanced analysis by decomposing the activations of LLMs into a sparse linear combination of SAE features. We introduce a novel metric to assess the monolinguality of features obtained from SAEs, discovering that some features are strongly related to specific languages. Additionally, we show that ablating these SAE features only significantly reduces abilities in one language of LLMs, leaving others almost unaffected. Interestingly, we find some languages have multiple synergistic SAE features, and ablating them together yields greater improvement than ablating individually. Moreover, we leverage these SAE-derived language-specific features to enhance steering vectors, achieving control over the language generated by LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aatrox103/multilingual-llm-features.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Does higher interpretability imply better utility? A Pairwise Analysis on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does higher interpretability of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features imply better steering utility for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds only a weak positive association between SAE feature interpretability and steering utility, and introduces a new feature selection criterion (∆Token Confidence) that significantly improves steering performance.
papers.conclusion: There is a significant divergence between SAE interpretability and steering utility, suggesting that prioritizing interpretability does not guarantee improved steering performance.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability shows a relatively weak positive association with steering utility (Kendall's τb ≈ 0.298).
∆Token Confidence effectively selects features with strong steering performance, improving steering score by 52.52% over the previous best method.
After selecting high-utility features with ∆Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes or becomes negative.
future_direction: Developing advanced post-training feature selection protocols or fundamentally new, utility-oriented SAE training paradigms.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to steer large language models (LLMs), based on the assumption that their interpretable features naturally enable effective model behavior steering. Yet, a fundamental question remains unanswered: does higher interpretability indeed imply better steering utility? To answer this question, we train 90 SAEs across three LLMs (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B, Gemma-2-9B), spanning five architectures and six sparsity levels, and evaluate their interpretability and steering utility based on SAEBench (arXiv:2501.12345) and AxBench (arXiv:2502.23456) respectively, and perform a rank-agreement analysis via Kendall's rank coefficients (tau b). Our analysis reveals only a relatively weak positive association (tau b approx 0.298), indicating that interpretability is an insufficient proxy for steering performance. We conjecture the interpretability utility gap may stem from the selection of SAE features, as not all of them are equally effective for steering. To further find features that truly steer the behavior of LLMs, we propose a novel selection criterion called Delta Token Confidence, which measures how much amplifying a feature changes the next token distribution. We show that our method improves the steering performance of three LLMs by 52.52 percent compared to the current best output score based criterion (arXiv:2503.34567). Strikingly, after selecting features with high Delta Token Confidence, the correlation between interpretability and utility vanishes (tau b approx 0), and can even become negative. This further highlights the divergence between interpretability and utility for the most effective steering features.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: A Survey on Sparse Autoencoders: Interpreting the Internal Mechanisms of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models. It covers technical frameworks, explanation methods, evaluation metrics, and applications.
papers.limitation:
Incomplete Concept Dictionary
Lack Theoretical Foundations
Reconstruction Errors
Computational Burden
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. Recently, mechanistic interpretability has attracted significant attention from the research community as a means to understand the inner workings of LLMs. Among various mechanistic interpretability approaches, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising method due to their ability to disentangle the complex, superimposed features within LLMs into more interpretable components. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of SAEs for interpreting and understanding the internal workings of LLMs. Our major contributions include: (1) exploring the technical framework of SAEs, covering basic architecture, design improvements, and effective training strategies; (2) examining different approaches to explaining SAE features, categorized into input-based and output-based explanation methods; (3) discussing evaluation methods for assessing SAE performance, covering both structural and functional metrics; and (4) investigating real-world applications of SAEs in understanding and manipulating LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Controllable LLM Reasoning via Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
papers.research_question: How can we control fine-grained reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models using Sparse Autoencoders to overcome concept entanglement and improve reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SAE-Steering, a method that uses Sparse Autoencoders to disentangle and identify strategy-specific features for controlling reasoning strategies in Large Reasoning Models, achieving superior control effectiveness and error correction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can disentangle strategy-specific features for fine-grained control of reasoning strategies, with SAE-Steering providing an efficient feature identification pipeline that is effective and robust.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-Steering outperforms existing control methods by over 15% in control effectiveness across various reasoning tasks and models.
The identified SAE features generalize from math to science domains, indicating cross-domain applicability.
Logit-based feature recall is more precise than activation-based methods, improving feature selection accuracy.
Strategy-specific features are prevalent in deeper layers of the model, with optimal control effectiveness in middle-to-late layers.
Controlling reasoning strategies can redirect models from erroneous paths, achieving a 7% absolute accuracy improvement in error correction.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated five representative reasoning strategies
Only demonstrated application in error correction scenarios
Only attempted to correct erroneous paths by enforcing continued reasoning
future_direction: Investigate controlling other reasoning strategies
Explore applying control to a wider range of applications
Explore guiding the LRM at earlier stages or during intermediate steps
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit human-like cognitive reasoning strategies (e.g. backtracking, cross-verification) during reasoning process, which improves their performance on complex tasks. Currently, reasoning strategies are autonomously selected by LRMs themselves. However, such autonomous selection often produces inefficient or even erroneous reasoning paths. To make reasoning more reliable and flexible, it is important to develop methods for controlling reasoning strategies. Existing methods struggle to control fine-grained reasoning strategies due to conceptual entanglement in LRMs' hidden states. To address this, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose strategy-entangled hidden states into a disentangled feature space. To identify the few strategy-specific features from the vast pool of SAE features, we propose SAE-Steering, an efficient two-stage feature identification pipeline. SAE-Steering first recalls features that amplify the logits of strategy-specific keywords, filtering out over 99\% of features, and then ranks the remaining features by their control effectiveness. Using the identified strategy-specific features as control vectors, SAE-Steering outperforms existing methods by over 15\% in control effectiveness. Furthermore, controlling reasoning strategies can redirect LRMs from erroneous paths to correct ones, achieving a 7\% absolute accuracy improvement.

papers.title: Measuring Sparse Autoencoder Feature Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How can we measure the sensitivity of Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features, i.e., how reliably they activate on texts similar to their activating examples?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a scalable, explanation-free method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity, demonstrating that sensitivity is a novel dimension of feature quality and that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity, with sensitivity declining as SAE width increases.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes feature sensitivity as a crucial dimension for evaluating both individual SAE features and SAE architectures, emphasizing the need for better sensitivity in scaled SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a generation-based method to evaluate SAE feature sensitivity without needing natural language descriptions.
Sensitivity measures a new aspect of feature quality, weakly correlated with existing metrics like interpretability and frequency.
Many interpretable SAE features have poor sensitivity, indicating they do not reliably activate on similar inputs.
Human evaluation confirms that generated text genuinely resembles activating examples when features fail to activate.
Average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants, highlighting a challenge in SAE scaling.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation limited to frequently occurring features, biasing analysis toward common features and missing rare features.
Filtering for features that remain active on truncated text may bias toward simpler features.
Does not incorporate activation magnitude into the sensitivity evaluation.
future_direction: Scale up evaluation to study less frequent features and use longer text snippets.
Incorporate activation strength into studies of SAE features.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features have become essential tools for mechanistic interpretability research. SAE features are typically characterized by examining their activating examples, which are often "monosemantic" and align with human interpretable concepts. However, these examples don't reveal feature sensitivity: how reliably a feature activates on texts similar to its activating examples. In this work, we develop a scalable method to evaluate feature sensitivity. Our approach avoids the need to generate natural language descriptions for features; instead we use language models to generate text with the same semantic properties as a feature's activating examples. We then test whether the feature activates on these generated texts. We demonstrate that sensitivity measures a new facet of feature quality and find that many interpretable features have poor sensitivity. Human evaluation confirms that when features fail to activate on our generated text, that text genuinely resembles the original activating examples. Lastly, we study feature sensitivity at the SAE level and observe that average feature sensitivity declines with increasing SAE width across 7 SAE variants. Our work establishes feature sensitivity as a new dimension for evaluating both individual features and SAE architectures.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Residual Stream Analysis with Multi-Layer SAEs
papers.research_question: How does information flow across layers in transformer language models, and can a single sparse autoencoder trained on residual stream activations from all layers capture this flow?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the multi-layer sparse autoencoder (MLSAE) trained on residual stream activations from every transformer layer, enabling study of information flow across layers and revealing that latents are often active at a single layer for a given token but can be active at different layers for different tokens.
papers.conclusion: MLSAEs provide a new approach to understanding how representations change as they flow through transformers, revealing patterns in latent activations across layers that depend on token aggregation and model size.
papers.key_findings:
MLSAEs achieve comparable reconstruction error and downstream loss to single-layer SAEs.
When aggregating over many tokens, individual latents are active at multiple layers, but for a single token, latent activations are more likely isolated to a single layer.
Larger underlying models have more similar residual stream activations at adjacent layers, and the degree to which latents are active at multiple layers increases with model size.
Applying pre-trained tuned-lens transformations to align layer bases does not obviously increase the extent of multi-layer latent activations.
The variance of latent activation distributions over layers is about two orders of magnitude greater when aggregating over tokens compared to a single token.
papers.limitation:
The data-stacked MLSAE approach may not capture 'cross-layer superposition' (simultaneous activations in multiple layers encoding a single concept) as effectively as a feature-stacked approach.
Pre-trained tuned lenses were not available for all models (e.g., Pythia-1b), limiting the scope of the tuned-lens experiments.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising approach to interpreting the internal representations of transformer language models. However, SAEs are usually trained separately on each transformer layer, making it difficult to use them to study how information flows across layers. To solve this problem, we introduce the multi-layer SAE (MLSAE): a single SAE trained on the residual stream activation vectors from every transformer layer. Given that the residual stream is understood to preserve information across layers, we expected MLSAE latents to 'switch on' at a token position and remain active at later layers. Interestingly, we find that individual latents are often active at a single layer for a given token or prompt, but the layer at which an individual latent is active may differ for different tokens or prompts. We quantify these phenomena by defining a distribution over layers and considering its variance. We find that the variance of the distributions of latent activations over layers is about two orders of magnitude greater when aggregating over tokens compared with a single token. For larger underlying models, the degree to which latents are active at multiple layers increases, which is consistent with the fact that the residual stream activation vectors at adjacent layers become more similar. Finally, we relax the assumption that the residual stream basis is the same at every layer by applying pre-trained tuned-lens transformations, but our findings remain qualitatively similar. Our results represent a new approach to understanding how representations change as they flow through transformers. We release our code to train and analyze MLSAEs at https://github.com/tim-lawson/mlsae.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can we identify functionally important features in neural networks? The paper investigates whether standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) learn features that are functionally important for network performance and proposes a new training method to ensure the features are functionally important.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces end-to-end sparse dictionary learning, a method for training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that ensures the learned features are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted.
papers.conclusion: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning offers a Pareto improvement over standard SAEs, requiring fewer features to explain network performance without sacrificing interpretability, bringing us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately.
papers.key_findings:
For the same level of performance explained, end-to-end SAEs require activating more than twice as few features per datapoint compared to standard SAEs.
End-to-end SAEs require fewer total features over the dataset to explain the same amount of network performance.
End-to-end SAEs with downstream reconstruction loss (SAEe2e+ds) achieve similar performance to SAEe2e while having activations that follow more similar pathways through the network compared to the original model.
The improved efficiency of end-to-end SAEs does not come at the cost of interpretability, as measured by automated interpretability scores and qualitative analysis.
End-to-end SAEs have more orthogonal features and are less prone to feature splitting compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation:
End-to-end SAEs take 2-3.5 times longer to train than standard SAEs.
There is a risk that SAEe2e may take different computational pathways through the network, though this is addressed by SAEe2e+ds.
The automated interpretability score is an imperfect metric of interpretability.
future_direction: Using training tweaks such as a sparsity schedule to allow for higher learning rates.
Using locally trained SAEs as initializations to reduce training time.
Training multiple SAEs at different layers concurrently to reduce training time.
papers.abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis at https://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE) and finds that it underperforms standard SAEs due to excessive KL divergence regularization causing feature death, disproving the hypothesis that variational methods improve feature organization.
papers.conclusion: The naive application of variational methods to sparse autoencoders does not improve feature organization or interpretability and is not a promising direction for SAE development.
papers.key_findings:
The vSAE underperforms the standard TopK SAE across core metrics like CE loss, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
The vSAE exhibits catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to KL divergence pressure pushing activations toward zero.
The vSAE shows improved performance on Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR) and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) benchmarks, indicating more independent features.
t-SNE visualizations reveal that vSAE features are more dispersed and less clustered than SAE features, supporting the dispersive pressure hypothesis.
Despite having far fewer active features, the vSAE maintains feature interpretability, but the overall performance degradation suggests variational methods are not beneficial for SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The vSAE suffers from catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to excessive KL divergence regularization.
