The analysis of SAEs with polysemous words can also figure out the internal mechanism of LLMs; deeper layers and the Attention module contribute to distinguishing polysemy in a word. Our semantics focused evaluation offers new insights into the polysemy and the existing SAE objective and contributes to the development of more practical SAEs.

papers.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the amortisation gap in sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and can more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that sparse autoencoder (SAE) encoders are inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference due to an amortisation gap, and demonstrates empirically that more expressive encoders (like MLPs) and sparse coding methods can outperform SAEs, leading to more interpretable features in large language models.
papers.conclusion: More sophisticated sparse inference methods, such as MLPs and sparse coding, can outperform traditional SAE encoders, reducing the amortisation gap and improving interpretability, which opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAE encoders have a provable amortisation gap, making them suboptimal for sparse inference even in solvable cases.
Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and sparse coding consistently outperform SAEs in recovering sparse codes, with sparse coding achieving the highest performance.
The performance advantage of more sophisticated methods is more pronounced in regimes where compressed sensing theory predicts recoverability.
These findings generalize to real-world applications, as shown by training on GPT-2 activations where MLPs yield more interpretable features than SAEs.
The amortisation gap can be reduced with increased compute, with MLPs surpassing SAE performance after a consistent computational threshold.
papers.limitation: The theoretical result on SAE suboptimality is proven for a specific setting (linear-nonlinear encoder, sparse signals in union of subspaces) and may not cover all practical SAE implementations.
future_direction: Pitting optimised sparse coding approaches (e.g., Least Angle Regression, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) against optimised SAE architectures.
Further exploration of top-k sparse coding with proper hyperparameter tuning to achieve Pareto improvements.
Scaling the methods to larger models and more complex datasets.
papers.abstract: A recent line of work has shown promise in using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to uncover interpretable features in neural network representations. However, the simple linear-nonlinear encoding mechanism in SAEs limits their ability to perform accurate sparse inference. Using compressed sensing theory, we prove that an SAE encoder is inherently insufficient for accurate sparse inference, even in solvable cases. We then decouple encoding and decoding processes to empirically explore conditions where more sophisticated sparse inference methods outperform traditional SAE encoders. Our results reveal substantial performance gains with minimal compute increases in correct inference of sparse codes. We demonstrate this generalises to SAEs applied to large language models, where more expressive encoders achieve greater interpretability. This work opens new avenues for understanding neural network representations and analysing large language model activations.

papers.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Does training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improve reconstruction fidelity and interpretability compared to broad-domain SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on a narrow domain (medical text) improves reconstruction fidelity, interpretability, and reduces linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggests the field may need to question 'foundation-model' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Domain-specific SAEs achieve 15-20% higher fraction of variance explained and better loss recovery than broad-domain SAEs.
Domain-specific SAEs produce features that are more interpretable and aligned with clinically meaningful concepts.
Domain-specific SAEs capture more linear structure, leaving a smaller and more nonlinear residual error (less dark matter).
Domain-specific SAEs show improved cosine similarity between activations and reconstructions.
Domain-specific SAEs have minimal shrinkage (relative reconstruction bias close to 1).
future_direction: Extending domain-specific SAEs to other specialised domains, such as legal or financial text.
Investigating how domain confinement affects feature splitting and absorption.
Studying the trade-offs between domain breadth and SAE performance.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose large language model (LLM) activations into latent features that reveal mechanistic structure. Conventional SAEs train on broad data distributions, forcing a fixed latent budget to capture only high-frequency, generic patterns. This often results in significant linear ``dark matter'' in reconstruction error and produces latents that fragment or absorb each other, complicating interpretation. We show that restricting SAE training to a well-defined domain (medical text) reallocates capacity to domain-specific features, improving both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability. Training JumpReLU SAEs on layer-20 activations of Gemma-2 models using 195k clinical QA examples, we find that domain-confined SAEs explain up to 20\% more variance, achieve higher loss recovery, and reduce linear residual error compared to broad-domain SAEs. Automated and human evaluations confirm that learned features align with clinically meaningful concepts (e.g., ``taste sensations'' or ``infectious mononucleosis''), rather than frequent but uninformative tokens. These domain-specific SAEs capture relevant linear structure, leaving a smaller, more purely nonlinear residual. We conclude that domain-confinement mitigates key limitations of broad-domain SAEs, enabling more complete and interpretable latent decompositions, and suggesting the field may need to question ``foundation-model'' scaling for general-purpose SAEs.

papers.title: Probing the Representational Power of Sparse Autoencoders in Vision Models
papers.research_question: How effective are Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting and steering vision models, and do they provide semantically meaningful features across different vision architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs extract semantically meaningful features from vision models, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable semantic steering in diffusion models, establishing SAEs as a valuable interpretability tool for vision.
papers.conclusion: SAE features are semantically meaningful and enhance interpretable understanding across vision encoders, multimodal LLMs, and diffusion models, highlighting SAEs as a unified interpretability tool across diverse vision architectures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features from vision encoders improve out-of-distribution generalization compared to original embeddings.
SAE features capture hierarchical semantic structures (ontological features) in image encoders.
SAEs enable semantic steering in diffusion models by manipulating text encoder features.
SAEs reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities in LMMs.
Different SAE variants (ReLU, TopK, Gated) show similar trends in reconstruction and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Findings on multimodal representation overlap in LMMs are preliminary and require future quantitative validation.
Steering Stable Diffusion 3.5 is more challenging due to its complex text encoding architecture.
future_direction: Quantitative validation of multimodal representation overlap in LMMs.
Systematic investigation of how visual representations evolve through LLM layers.
Future application of SAEs in vision models.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a popular tool for interpreting the hidden states of large language models (LLMs). By learning to reconstruct activations from a sparse bottleneck layer, SAEs discover interpretable features from the high-dimensional internal representations of LLMs. Despite their popularity with language models, SAEs remain understudied in the visual domain. In this work, we provide an extensive evaluation the representational power of SAEs for vision models using a broad range of image-based tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that SAE features are semantically meaningful, improve out-of-distribution generalization, and enable controllable generation across three vision model architectures: vision embedding models, multi-modal LMMs and diffusion models. In vision embedding models, we find that learned SAE features can be used for OOD detection and provide evidence that they recover the ontological structure of the underlying model. For diffusion models, we demonstrate that SAEs enable semantic steering through text encoder manipulation and develop an automated pipeline for discovering human-interpretable attributes. Finally, we conduct exploratory experiments on multi-modal LLMs, finding evidence that SAE features reveal shared representations across vision and language modalities. Our study provides a foundation for SAE evaluation in vision models, highlighting their strong potential improving interpretability, generalization, and steerability in the visual domain.

papers.title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Switch Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders efficiently to reduce compute cost while maintaining performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture that uses a mixture-of-experts style routing to reduce compute cost and memory bottlenecks while maintaining reconstruction performance and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Switch SAEs are a promising approach for scaling sparse autoencoders, providing a Pareto improvement in FLOPs vs. MSE without significant reduction in feature interpretability, and may enable large-scale SAE training on GPU clusters.
papers.key_findings:
Switch SAEs achieve better reconstruction than dense TopK SAEs at a fixed compute budget (FLOP-matched).
Switch SAEs require more total features (parameters) to achieve the same reconstruction as dense SAEs when trained to convergence, but this gap narrows for larger SAEs.
In FLOP-matched settings, Switch SAEs Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated, and ReLU SAEs in terms of reconstruction MSE and fraction of loss recovered.
Switch SAEs exhibit feature duplication across experts, which reduces capacity, but this effect diminishes at larger sparsities.
Switch SAE features are as interpretable as TopK SAE features in FLOP-matched settings, and in width-matched settings they have higher true positive rates but lower true negative rates in automated interpretability detection.
papers.limitation:
Switch SAEs have reduced performance at a fixed number of parameters compared to dense SAEs, especially for attention and MLP layers.
Only the simplest mixture-of-experts architecture is investigated, leaving open the question of maximum performance gain from more sophisticated MoE architectures.
No downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs (e.g., feature steering or circuit discovery) are conducted.
future_direction: Investigate feature deduplication techniques, more sophisticated routing architectures, and multiple active experts.
Explore more sophisticated mixture-of-experts architectures like GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert choice routing.
Conduct downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs, such as feature steering or circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a recent technique for decomposing neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, in order for SAEs to identify all features represented in frontier models, it will be necessary to scale them up to very high width, posing a computational challenge. In this work, we introduce Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture aimed at reducing the compute cost of training SAEs. Inspired by sparse mixture of experts models, Switch SAEs route activation vectors between smaller "expert" SAEs, enabling SAEs to efficiently scale to many more features. We present experiments comparing Switch SAEs with other SAE architectures, and find that Switch SAEs deliver a substantial Pareto improvement in the reconstruction vs. sparsity frontier for a given fixed training compute budget. We also study the geometry of features across experts, analyze features duplicated across experts, and verify that Switch SAE features are as interpretable as features found by other SAE architectures.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Trained on the Same Data Learn Different Features
papers.research_question: Does the random seed used to initialize sparse autoencoders affect the features they learn when trained on the same data and model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs trained on the same data and model with different random seeds learn different features, suggesting that SAE features are not universal but rather pragmatic decompositions of activation space.
papers.conclusion: SAEs do not uncover a universal set of features; feature discovery should be viewed as a compositional, hierarchical problem due to the nonconvexity of the loss function.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained with different random seeds identify different sets of features, with only 30% shared in Llama 3 8B.
Shared features tend to fire more frequently and are more interpretable than orphan features.
Orphan features can still be interpretable, indicating that individual SAE runs may miss interpretable features.
Feature overlap decreases with more SAE latents and increases with longer training time.
ReLU SAEs with L1 loss show greater stability across seeds compared to TopK SAEs.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a useful tool for uncovering human-interpretable features in the activations of large language models (LLMs). While some expect SAEs to find the true underlying features used by a model, our research shows that SAEs trained on the same model and data, differing only in the random seed used to initialize their weights, identify different sets of features. For example, in an SAE with 131K latents trained on a feedforward network in Llama 3 8B, only 30% of the features were shared across different seeds. We observed this phenomenon across multiple layers of three different LLMs, two datasets, and several SAE architectures. While ReLU SAEs trained with the L1 sparsity loss showed greater stability across seeds, SAEs using the state-of-the-art TopK activation function were more seed-dependent, even when controlling for the level of sparsity. Our results suggest that the set of features uncovered by an SAE should be viewed as a pragmatically useful decomposition of activation space, rather than an exhaustive and universal list of features "truly used" by the model.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering LLMs with Mutual Information-based Explanations on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to better explain sparse autoencoder features in LLMs to capture semantic meaning and use these explanations to steer LLM behaviors, particularly for defending against jailbreak attacks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based explanation method for sparse autoencoder features that mitigates frequency bias and enables effective steering of LLM behaviors, particularly for enhancing safety against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that discourse-level explanations from sparse autoencoders are crucial for understanding and steering LLM behaviors, particularly for safety applications.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical analysis reveals frequency bias in sparse autoencoder features between discourse topics and linguistic patterns.
The proposed mutual information-based method generates more discourse-level explanations compared to baseline methods like TopAct and N2G.
The discourse-level explanations are effective in steering LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks.
Experiments show a higher successful explained rate for features with the proposed method.
Steering strategies such as amplification and calibration can enhance LLM safety without additional model training.
papers.limitation: The approach relies on existing sparse autoencoders without modifying their architectures or training to mitigate frequency bias.
future_direction: Designing improved architectures or training objectives for sparse autoencoders to inherently mitigate frequency bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at handling human queries, but they can occasionally generate flawed or unexpected responses. Understanding their internal states is crucial for understanding their successes, diagnosing their failures, and refining their capabilities. Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for interpreting LLM internal representations, limited research has explored how to better explain SAE features, i.e., understanding the semantic meaning of features learned by SAE. Our theoretical analysis reveals that existing explanation methods suffer from the frequency bias issue, where they emphasize linguistic patterns over semantic concepts, while the latter is more critical to steer LLM behaviors. To address this, we propose using a fixed vocabulary set for feature interpretations and designing a mutual information-based objective, aiming to better capture the semantic meaning behind these features. We further propose two runtime steering strategies that adjust the learned feature activations based on their corresponding explanations. Empirical results show that, compared to baselines, our method provides more discourse-level explanations and effectively steers LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks. These findings highlight the value of explanations for steering LLM behaviors in downstream applications. We will release our code and data once accepted.

papers.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What causes Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fail in recovering true underlying features when the features form a hierarchy? The paper identifies and studies the phenomenon of feature absorption.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes the phenomenon of feature absorption in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), showing it is caused by hierarchical features and the sparsity penalty, and introduces a metric to detect it.
papers.conclusion: Feature absorption poses an obstacle to the practical application of SAEs for interpretability, and fundamental theoretical issues need to be addressed before SAEs can be used robustly at scale.
papers.key_findings:
Feature absorption occurs in SAEs when features form a hierarchy, causing seemingly monosemantic latents to fail to fire where they should.
The phenomenon is caused by the sparsity penalty in SAEs.
The paper proposes a metric to detect feature absorption and validates it on hundreds of LLM SAEs.
Feature absorption is widespread and occurs in every LLM SAE tested.
Varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve the issue.
papers.limitation:
The absorption metric is limited to early layers (before layer 18 in Gemma 2 2B) because attention moves information to later tokens, making causal interventions ineffective at later layers.
The absorption metric is likely an underestimate of true absorption because it only captures cases where a single latent dominates and the main latents are fully turned off.
future_direction: Develop improved metrics for feature absorption that can be applied at all model layers and capture partial absorption.
Address the fundamental theoretical issues causing feature absorption to enable robust use of SAEs for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) aim to decompose the activation space of large language models (LLMs) into human-interpretable latent directions or features. As we increase the number of features in the SAE, hierarchical features tend to split into finer features ("math" may split into "algebra", "geometry", etc.), a phenomenon referred to as feature splitting. However, we show that sparse decomposition and splitting of hierarchical features is not robust. Specifically, we show that seemingly monosemantic features fail to fire where they should, and instead get "absorbed" into their children features. We coin this phenomenon feature absorption, and show that it is caused by optimizing for sparsity in SAEs whenever the underlying features form a hierarchy. We introduce a metric to detect absorption in SAEs, and validate our findings empirically on hundreds of LLM SAEs. Our investigation suggests that varying SAE sizes or sparsity is insufficient to solve this issue. We discuss the implications of feature absorption in SAEs and some potential approaches to solve the fundamental theoretical issues before SAEs can be used for interpreting LLMs robustly and at scale.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders: From Shallow Design to Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the limitations of shallow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in extracting correlated features due to an implicit quasi-orthogonality assumption, and proposes an iterative SAE based on Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE) to overcome these limitations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, an iterative sparse autoencoder that unrolls Matching Pursuit, which improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs by enabling residual-guided extraction of correlated features.
papers.conclusion: MP-SAE improves expressivity, learns hierarchical features, and overcomes the coherence limitations of shallow SAEs, providing a foundation for building more interpretable sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
MP-SAE is more expressive than shallow SAEs across varying sparsity levels and dictionary sizes.
MP-SAE learns a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine feature structure, with early atoms capturing digit prototypes and later atoms refining pen strokes.
MP-SAE learns a globally coherent dictionary but selects more incoherent subsets of atoms during inference, unlike shallow SAEs where dictionary and selected atom coherence align.
MP-SAE guarantees monotonic improvement in reconstruction as more atoms are selected, a property not shared by other SAEs.
Shallow SAEs (ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, BatchTopK) exhibit distinct structural biases in their learned dictionaries, such as ReLU learning full-digit atoms and others learning pen-stroke patterns.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently become central tools for interpretability, leveraging dictionary learning principles to extract sparse, interpretable features from neural representations whose underlying structure is typically unknown. This paper evaluates SAEs in a controlled setting using MNIST, which reveals that current shallow architectures implicitly rely on a quasi-orthogonality assumption that limits the ability to extract correlated features. To move beyond this, we compare them with an iterative SAE that unrolls Matching Pursuit (MP-SAE), enabling the residual-guided extraction of correlated features that arise in hierarchical settings such as handwritten digit generation while guaranteeing monotonic improvement of the reconstruction as more atoms are selected.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret the internal representations of protein language models and steer them to generate sequences with desired features?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that sparse autoencoders can be applied to protein language models to interpret their internal representations and that the identified latent features can be used to steer the model to generate protein sequences with desired structural motifs.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising approach for interpreting and controlling protein language models, opening new avenues for protein design and engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders trained on ESM-2 activations can identify latent components associated with protein annotations such as transmembrane regions, binding sites, and zinc finger motifs.
A heuristic based on intrinsic dimension estimation can guide the selection of the transformer layer from which to extract representations for SAE training.
Intervening on specific latent components during inference can steer the model to generate protein sequences that contain desired features, such as zinc finger domains.
The sequence generation pipeline successfully produced sequences with zinc finger motifs, though it requires parameter tuning to improve success rates.
papers.limitation:
The sequence generation pipeline requires parameter fine-tuning to improve the success rate.
The features learned by the model may not directly align with manually curated dataset annotations, as latents might encode more specific or coarse-grained features.
future_direction: Extend these methods to larger models and a wider range of protein features.
Automate the parameter search for the sequence generation pipeline to improve efficiency.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancements in transformer-based language models have revolutionized natural language processing, yet understanding the internal mechanisms of these models remains a significant challenge. This paper explores the application of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to interpret the internal representations of protein language models, specifically focusing on the ESM-2 8M parameter model. By performing a statistical analysis on each latent component's relevance to distinct protein annotations, we identify potential interpretations linked to various protein characteristics, including transmembrane regions, binding sites, and specialized motifs. We then leverage these insights to guide sequence generation, shortlisting the relevant latent components that can steer the model towards desired targets such as zinc finger domains. This work contributes to the emerging field of mechanistic interpretability in biological sequence models, offering new perspectives on model steering for sequence design.

papers.title: Mechanistic Knobs in LLMs: Retrieving and Steering High-Order Semantic Features via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can internal features in Large Language Models be linked to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering high-order semantic features in LLMs, enabling precise, bidirectional behavior control and identifying the Functional Faithfulness effect where interventions induce coherent shifts across linguistic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, providing a robust mechanistic path for regulating complex AI behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-based features allow precise steering of personality traits in LLMs, enabling bidirectional control.
The method outperforms Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) in stability and performance, with higher validity rates.
Functional Faithfulness effect is observed where steering on a feature induces systematic behavioral shifts aligned with the target semantic attribute.
Retrieved features are semantically interpretable and causally effective for model behavior regulation.
LLM internal representations of personality traits align with human psychological frameworks, as shown through social intelligence evaluations.
papers.abstract: Recent work in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has enabled the identification and intervention of internal features in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, a persistent challenge lies in linking such internal features to the reliable control of complex, behavior-level semantic attributes in language generation. In this paper, we propose a Sparse Autoencoder-based framework for retrieving and steering semantically interpretable internal features associated with high-level linguistic behaviors. Our method employs a contrastive feature retrieval pipeline based on controlled semantic oppositions, combing statistical activation analysis and generation-based validation to distill monosemantic functional features from sparse activation spaces. Using the Big Five personality traits as a case study, we demonstrate that our method enables precise, bidirectional steering of model behavior while maintaining superior stability and performance compared to existing activation steering methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). We further identify an empirical effect, which we term Functional Faithfulness, whereby intervening on a specific internal feature induces coherent and predictable shifts across multiple linguistic dimensions aligned with the target semantic attribute. Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the interpretability and steerability of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) by incorporating user-specified concepts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE), a framework that prunes low-utility SAE neurons and augments the latent space with a concept bottleneck aligned to user-defined concepts, improving interpretability and steerability.
papers.conclusion: CB-SAE unifies sparse autoencoders with concept bottleneck models, enabling robust interpretation and control of vision representations across modalities and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Most SAE neurons have low interpretability or steerability, rendering them ineffective for downstream use.
SAEs often fail to represent user-specified concepts, limiting their practical utility.
CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% over SAE baselines across LVLMs and image generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) promise a unified approach for mechanistic interpretability, concept discovery, and model steering in LLMs and LVLMs. However, realizing this potential requires that the learned features be both interpretable and steerable. To that end, we introduce two new computationally inexpensive interpretability and steerability metrics and conduct a systematic analysis on LVLMs. Our analysis uncovers two observations; (i) a majority of SAE neurons exhibit either low interpretability or low steerability or both, rendering them ineffective for downstream use; and (ii) due to the unsupervised nature of SAEs, user-desired concepts are often absent in the learned dictionary, thus limiting their practical utility. To address these limitations, we propose Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders (CB-SAE) - a novel post-hoc framework that prunes low-utility neurons and augments the latent space with a lightweight concept bottleneck aligned to a user-defined concept set. The resulting CB-SAE improves interpretability by +32.1% and steerability by +14.5% across LVLMs and image generation tasks. We will make our code and model weights available.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders to large language models and how should we evaluate their quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for scaling sparse autoencoders using a TopK activation function to directly control sparsity and techniques to prevent dead latents, establishes scaling laws, and proposes new metrics for evaluating feature quality.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can be scaled effectively with the proposed methods, and larger autoencoders yield better features according to the introduced evaluation metrics.
papers.key_findings:
TopK activation function improves the reconstruction-sparsity frontier and simplifies training compared to ReLU autoencoders with L1 penalty.
Techniques like tied initialization and an auxiliary loss reduce dead latents to 7% in a 16 million latent autoencoder.
Clean scaling laws are found with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity.
Larger autoencoders generally improve feature quality according to new metrics (probe loss, explainability, ablation sparsity).
The method scales to training a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations.
papers.limitation:
The probe-based evaluation metric leans on strong assumptions about what kinds of features are natural.
Evaluating explanation precision for arbitrary English explanations is computationally expensive.
future_direction: Explore ways to make it more tractable to approximate precision for arbitrary English explanations.
Scale to even larger autoencoders and apply the method to other models and modalities.
Improve evaluation metrics for feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders provide a promising unsupervised approach for extracting interpretable features from a language model by reconstructing activations from a sparse bottleneck layer. Since language models learn many concepts, autoencoders need to be very large to recover all relevant features. However, studying the properties of autoencoder scaling is difficult due to the need to balance reconstruction and sparsity objectives and the presence of dead latents. We propose using k-sparse autoencoders [Makhzani and Frey, 2013] to directly control sparsity, simplifying tuning and improving the reconstruction-sparsity frontier. Additionally, we find modifications that result in few dead latents, even at the largest scales we tried. Using these techniques, we find clean scaling laws with respect to autoencoder size and sparsity. We also introduce several new metrics for evaluating feature quality based on the recovery of hypothesized features, the explainability of activation patterns, and the sparsity of downstream effects. These metrics all generally improve with autoencoder size. To demonstrate the scalability of our approach, we train a 16 million latent autoencoder on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens. We release training code and autoencoders for open-source models, as well as a visualizer.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: DLM-Scope: Mechanistic Interpretability of Diffusion Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders (SAEs) be used for mechanistic interpretability in diffusion language models (DLMs), and how do their properties and applications differ from those in autoregressive LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), demonstrating that SAEs can extract interpretable features, enable effective diffusion-time steering, analyze decoding order, and transfer from base to instruction-tuned models.
papers.conclusion: DLM-Scope establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows the great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on DLMs achieve a favorable sparsity-fidelity trade-off and can even reduce cross-entropy loss when inserted in early layers, a phenomenon absent or weaker in LLMs.
SAE features enable effective diffusion-time interventions (steering) that often outperform single-pass LLM steering.
SAE feature dynamics provide a useful signal for analyzing and correlating with the performance of different DLM decoding-order strategies.
Base-trained SAEs transfer almost losslessly to instruction-tuned DLMs in shallow and middle layers, but not in the deepest layer, indicating tuning-specific changes in deep representations.
future_direction: As DLMs scale, we plan to extend SAEs to more DLMs to better understand and improve models.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a standard tool for mechanistic interpretability in autoregressive large language models (LLMs), enabling researchers to extract sparse, human-interpretable features and intervene on model behavior. Recently, as diffusion language models (DLMs) have become an increasingly promising alternative to the autoregressive LLMs, it is essential to develop tailored mechanistic interpretability tools for this emerging class of models. In this work, we present DLM-Scope, the first SAE-based interpretability framework for DLMs, and demonstrate that trained Top-K SAEs can faithfully extract interpretable features. Notably, we find that inserting SAEs affects DLMs differently than autoregressive LLMs: while SAE insertion in LLMs typically incurs a loss penalty, in DLMs it can reduce cross-entropy loss when applied to early layers, a phenomenon absent or markedly weaker in LLMs. Additionally, SAE features in DLMs enable more effective diffusion-time interventions, often outperforming LLM steering. Moreover, we pioneer certain new SAE-based research directions for DLMs: we show that SAEs can provide useful signals for DLM decoding order; and the SAE features are stable during the post-training phase of DLMs. Our work establishes a foundation for mechanistic interpretability in DLMs and shows a great potential of applying SAEs to DLM-related tasks and algorithms.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Understanding sparse autoencoder scaling in the presence of feature manifolds
papers.research_question: How do feature manifolds influence the scaling behavior of sparse autoencoders, and can they cause pathological scaling where SAEs allocate too many latents to common manifolds at the expense of discovering rarer features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts a capacity-allocation model to sparse autoencoders, revealing that feature manifolds can lead to pathological scaling where SAEs allocate excessive latents to common manifolds, potentially hindering feature discovery.
papers.conclusion: The work frames the problem of SAE scaling and identifies conditions for pathological scaling, but it remains uncertain whether real SAEs are in this regime due to unknown feature geometry and frequency distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The model recovers distinct scaling regimes for SAEs: one where feature discovery keeps pace with latent count, and another where latents accumulate on common feature manifolds.
When the per-feature loss scaling exponent β is less than the feature frequency exponent α, SAEs enter a pathological regime where they learn far fewer features than the number of latents.
Experiments on synthetic manifolds show that the loss scaling curve depends on manifold geometry; some manifolds allow gradual loss reduction with more latents, while others saturate quickly.
Analysis of real SAEs (Gemma Scope and Inception-v1) shows some latents with high cosine similarity, but evidence for pathological tiling is inconclusive.
The presence of radial variation in feature manifolds may cause SAEs to learn basis-like solutions rather than tiling, suggesting pathological scaling might not occur in practice.
papers.limitation:
The assumptions of feature-specific latents, decoder respect for subspaces, and orthogonal feature subspaces may not hold in practice (e.g., due to feature absorption and non-orthogonality).
The model assumes power-law distributions for feature frequencies and loss scaling, which may not accurately reflect real data.
The question of whether SAEs are in the pathological regime is not resolved due to uncertainty about real feature geometries and frequencies.
future_direction: Estimating the feature frequency exponent α and loss scaling exponent β for real SAEs.
Studying the geometry of real feature manifolds to better understand SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) model the activations of a neural network as linear combinations of sparsely occurring directions of variation (latents). The ability of SAEs to reconstruct activations follows scaling laws w.r.t. the number of latents. In this work, we adapt a capacity-allocation model from the neural scaling literature (Brill, 2024) to understand SAE scaling, and in particular, to understand how "feature manifolds" (multi-dimensional features) influence scaling behavior. Consistent with prior work, the model recovers distinct scaling regimes. Notably, in one regime, feature manifolds have the pathological effect of causing SAEs to learn far fewer features in data than there are latents in the SAE. We provide some preliminary discussion on whether or not SAEs are in this pathological regime in the wild.

papers.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to identify and analyze language-specific features in multilingual Large Language Models, and what is the impact of these features on model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify language-specific features in LLMs and demonstrates that these features can be used to enhance steering vectors for better control over the language generated by the models.
papers.conclusion: The study uses SAEs to analyze multilingual capabilities in LLMs, identifying language-specific features that play a crucial role in language generation and can be leveraged to enhance steering vectors for improved language control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can exhibit strong monolingual characteristics, as measured by a novel monolinguality metric.
Language-specific features are not only tied to language-specific tokens but also to the language-specific linguistic context, as shown in code-switching experiments.
Ablating language-specific features via directional ablation significantly reduces model performance only in the target language, leaving other languages largely unaffected.
Some languages have multiple synergistic features; ablating them together yields a greater performance impact than ablating them individually.
Using language-specific features as gating signals to improve steering vectors achieves better control over the language generated by LLMs, with improved performance and robustness.
papers.limitation:
The method does not yet cover certain low-resource languages.
The SAE-based steering vectors sometimes underperform compared to the original steering vectors.
The SAEs used were not trained on curated multilingual data.
future_direction: Utilize language-specific features to guide the training process of multilingual language models.
Investigate low-resource languages to enhance the analysis.
Explore more refined approaches to improve the performance of SAE-based steering vectors.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms behind multilingual capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) have been examined using neuron-based or internal-activation-based methods. However, these methods often face challenges such as superposition and layer-wise activation variance, which limit their reliability. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) offer a more nuanced analysis by decomposing the activations of LLMs into a sparse linear combination of SAE features. We introduce a novel metric to assess the monolinguality of features obtained from SAEs, discovering that some features are strongly related to specific languages. Additionally, we show that ablating these SAE features only significantly reduces abilities in one language of LLMs, leaving others almost unaffected. Interestingly, we find some languages have multiple synergistic SAE features, and ablating them together yields greater improvement than ablating individually. Moreover, we leverage these SAE-derived language-specific features to enhance steering vectors, achieving control over the language generated by LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aatrox103/multilingual-llm-features.

papers.title: Denoising Concept Vectors with Sparse Autoencoders for Improved Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of linear concept vectors for language model steering by denoising hidden representations using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SDCV, a method that uses sparse autoencoders to denoise hidden representations by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples, leading to improved steering success rates.
papers.conclusion: SDCV effectively mitigates noise in concept vectors and enhances steering performance, demonstrating that denoising representations is a promising direction for robust concept steering.
papers.key_findings:
SDCV improves steering success rates by 4-16% across six challenging concepts while maintaining topic relevance.
SDCV-enhanced difference-in-mean generally outperforms SDCV-enhanced linear probing.
The method is effective across different models (Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-2B).
Optimal values for top-k and scale factor are not linearly related to peak performance, likely due to superposition and SAE training objectives.
Counterfactual experiments show that amplifying non-top-k latents (noise) generally decreases steering success.
papers.limitation:
The approach is confined to model families for which SAEs have already been trained.
SAEs imperfectly disentangle features and struggle to accurately capture feature importance.
Optimal values for steering strength, k, and scale factor must be determined empirically, which is computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: Linear concept vectors effectively steer LLMs, but existing methods suffer from noisy features in diverse datasets that undermine steering robustness. We propose Sparse Autoencoder-Denoised Concept Vectors (SDCV), which selectively keep the most discriminative SAE latents while reconstructing hidden representations. Our key insight is that concept-relevant signals can be explicitly separated from dataset noise by scaling up activations of top-k latents that best differentiate positive and negative samples. Applied to linear probing and difference-in-mean, SDCV consistently improves steering success rates by 4-16\% across six challenging concepts, while maintaining topic relevance.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: AbsTopK: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders For Bidirectional Features
papers.research_question: Is the use of nonnegative activations truly essential for the success of SAEs, or does it constrain their ability to capture richer representations? Can SAEs be improved by allowing negative activations, enabling the discovery of bidirectional concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AbsTopK SAE, a sparse autoencoder variant that removes the non-negativity constraint, enabling single latent features to encode bidirectional semantic concepts and improving reconstruction fidelity and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Removing the non-negativity constraint in SAEs via the AbsTopK operator allows single features to capture bipolar semantics and yields reconstructions of superior compactness and fidelity, pioneering a shift towards bipolar sparse representations.
papers.key_findings:
AbsTopK SAE enables single latent features to encode opposing concepts by leveraging both positive and negative activations.
AbsTopK outperforms TopK and JumpReLU SAEs in reconstruction fidelity and interpretability across multiple models and tasks.
AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the supervised Difference-in-Mean method on some steering tasks.
The non-negativity constraint in existing SAEs fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness.
AbsTopK achieves a better balance between safety alignment (HarmBench) and general capability preservation (MMLU) compared to conventional SAE steering.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-step variants, yielding multi-layer encoders that produce more accurate sparse codes.
Investigating JumpReLU variants that apply a threshold on both positive and negative activations.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as powerful techniques for interpretability of large language models (LLMs), aiming to decompose hidden states into meaningful semantic features. While several SAE variants have been proposed, there remains no principled framework to derive SAEs from the original dictionary learning formulation. In this work, we introduce such a framework by unrolling the proximal gradient method for sparse coding. We show that a single-step update naturally recovers common SAE variants, including ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. Through this lens, we reveal a fundamental limitation of existing SAEs: their sparsity-inducing regularizers enforce non-negativity, preventing a single feature from representing bidirectional concepts (e.g., male vs. female). This structural constraint fragments semantic axes into separate, redundant features, limiting representational completeness. To address this issue, we propose AbsTopK SAE, a new variant derived from the $\ell_0$ sparsity constraint that applies hard thresholding over the largest-magnitude activations. By preserving both positive and negative activations, AbsTopK uncovers richer, bidirectional conceptual representations. Comprehensive experiments across four LLMs and seven probing and steering tasks show that AbsTopK improves reconstruction fidelity, enhances interpretability, and enables single features to encode contrasting concepts. Remarkably, AbsTopK matches or even surpasses the Difference-in-Mean method, a supervised approach that requires labeled data for each concept and has been shown in prior work to outperform SAEs.

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: From Flat to Hierarchical: Extracting Sparse Representations with Matching Pursuit
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural network representations, and whether a new SAE architecture (MP-SAE) can better capture such structures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MP-SAE, a sparse autoencoder based on matching pursuit, which captures hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features in neural representations, outperforming existing SAEs and revealing cross-modal structure in vision-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability methods should be grounded in the phenomenology of representations, and that MP-SAE provides a step in this direction by capturing hierarchical and nonlinear structures.
papers.key_findings:
Existing SAEs struggle to capture conditionally orthogonal (hierarchical) features, while MP-SAE can capture both intra-level and inter-level structure.
MP-SAE recovers more expressive features than standard SAEs across various vision models, achieving higher reconstruction accuracy at comparable sparsity.
MP-SAE enables adaptive sparsity at inference time, allowing monotonic improvement in reconstruction error with each step, unlike fixed-sparsity SAEs.
MP-SAE learns dictionaries with higher global coherence but selects less interfering features at inference, promoting conditional orthogonality.
MP-SAE uncovers multimodal features in vision-language models that are shared across modalities, whereas standard SAEs tend to learn modality-specific features.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to hierarchical and nonlinear structures; other forms of structure (e.g., multi-dimensional features) are not addressed.
MP-SAE's inference requires multiple steps, which may be computationally more expensive than standard SAEs.
future_direction: Extending MP-SAE to capture multi-dimensional features.
Applying MP-SAE to larger-scale language models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the hypothesis that neural network representations encode abstract, interpretable features as linearly accessible, approximately orthogonal directions, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a popular tool in interpretability. However, recent work has demonstrated phenomenology of model representations that lies outside the scope of this hypothesis, showing signatures of hierarchical, nonlinear, and multi-dimensional features. This raises the question: do SAEs represent features that possess structure at odds with their motivating hypothesis? If not, does avoiding this mismatch help identify said features and gain further insights into neural network representations? To answer these questions, we take a construction-based approach and re-contextualize the popular matching pursuits (MP) algorithm from sparse coding to design MP-SAE -- an SAE that unrolls its encoder into a sequence of residual-guided steps, allowing it to capture hierarchical and nonlinearly accessible features. Comparing this architecture with existing SAEs on a mixture of synthetic and natural data settings, we show: (i) hierarchical concepts induce conditionally orthogonal features, which existing SAEs are unable to faithfully capture, and (ii) the nonlinear encoding step of MP-SAE recovers highly meaningful features, helping us unravel shared structure in the seemingly dichotomous representation spaces of different modalities in a vision-language model, hence demonstrating the assumption that useful features are solely linearly accessible is insufficient. We also show that the sequential encoder principle of MP-SAE affords an additional benefit of adaptive sparsity at inference time, which may be of independent interest. Overall, we argue our results provide credence to the idea that interpretability should begin with the phenomenology of representations, with methods emerging from assumptions that fit it.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
