papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: SplInterp: Improving our Understanding and Training of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the theoretical understanding and training of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) using spline theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies spline theory to understand SAEs, showing they are piecewise affine splines that generalize k-means autoencoders, and introduces the PAM-SGD training algorithm which improves sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.conclusion: The spline theory lens provides insight into SAEs, and PAM-SGD is a promising training method with advantages in sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are piecewise affine splines, and TopK SAEs correspond to Kth-order power diagrams.
SAEs generalize k-means autoencoders but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability compared to the optimal piecewise affine autoencoder (which combines k-means with local PCA).
The proposed PAM-SGD algorithm for training SAEs has solid theoretical foundations and shows promising empirical results, especially in low-data regimes and improved sparsity.
papers.limitation:
The spline geometry characterization is currently limited to TopK SAEs.
The bridge between SAEs and PCA-based autoencoders sets aside the matter of shared decoding vectors.
PAM-SGD makes approximations that break assumptions of the theory and had some empirical limitations (e.g., instability with TopK in LLM experiments).
future_direction: Extending the spline geometry characterization beyond TopK SAEs.
Exploring the incorporation of geometry into SAE training.
Studying the optimal autoencoding with shared decoding vectors and understanding more deeply the pros and cons of PAM-SGD.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have received considerable recent attention as tools for mechanistic interpretability, showing success at extracting interpretable features even from very large LLMs. However, this research has been largely empirical, and there have been recent doubts about the true utility of SAEs. In this work, we seek to enhance the theoretical understanding of SAEs, using the spline theory of deep learning. By situating SAEs in this framework: we discover that SAEs generalise ``$k$-means autoencoders'' to be piecewise affine, but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability vs. the optimal ``$k$-means-esque plus local principal component analysis (PCA)'' piecewise affine autoencoder. We characterise the underlying geometry of (TopK) SAEs using power diagrams. And we develop a novel proximal alternating method SGD (PAM-SGD) algorithm for training SAEs, with both solid theoretical foundations and promising empirical results in MNIST and LLM experiments, particularly in sample efficiency and (in the LLM setting) improved sparsity of codes. All code is available at: https://github.com/splInterp2025/splInterp

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
papers.research_question: Do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) improve performance on LLM activation probing tasks in challenging regimes such as data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift?
papers.core_contribution: SAE probes do not consistently outperform baseline probing methods across various challenging regimes, and baseline methods can achieve similar interpretability insights.
papers.conclusion: Current SAEs do not offer a consistent advantage for probing tasks, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation of interpretability methods with strong baselines.
papers.key_findings:
SAE probes underperform baseline logistic regression on average across datasets in standard conditions.
SAE probes do not provide a consistent advantage in data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift regimes.
Baseline methods can provide similar interpretability insights as SAE probes, such as detecting dataset issues.
Pruning SAE latents based on autointerp descriptions can slightly improve out-of-distribution generalization but not enough to match the performance drop.
SAE latents sometimes fail to generalize out-of-distribution, e.g., a latent for 'living room' only fires on English phrases.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to probing tasks and may not generalize to other tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for interpreting concepts represented in large language model (LLM) activations. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the validity of their interpretations due to the lack of a ground truth for the concepts used by an LLM, and a growing number of works have presented problems with current SAEs. One alternative source of evidence would be demonstrating that SAEs improve performance on downstream tasks beyond existing baselines. We test this by applying SAEs to the real-world task of LLM activation probing in four regimes: data scarcity, class imbalance, label noise, and covariate shift. Due to the difficulty of detecting concepts in these challenging settings, we hypothesize that SAEs' basis of interpretable, concept-level latents should provide a useful inductive bias. However, although SAEs occasionally perform better than baselines on individual datasets, we are unable to design ensemble methods combining SAEs with baselines that consistently outperform ensemble methods solely using baselines. Additionally, although SAEs initially appear promising for identifying spurious correlations, detecting poor dataset quality, and training multi-token probes, we are able to achieve similar results with simple non-SAE baselines as well. Though we cannot discount SAEs' utility on other tasks, our findings highlight the shortcomings of current SAEs and the need to rigorously evaluate interpretability methods on downstream tasks with strong baselines.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Temporal Difference Learning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models implement temporal difference learning to solve reinforcement learning problems in-context, despite being trained only for next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders can reveal and causally manipulate these representations.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that large language models implement temporal difference learning for in-context reinforcement learning, and sparse autoencoders provide a methodology for studying and manipulating these mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 3 70B can solve simple reinforcement learning problems in-context and its behavior is best described by a Q-learning model.
Sparse autoencoders trained on the residual stream reveal features that correlate with temporal difference errors and Q-values.
Intervening on these temporal difference features (lesioning or clamping) impairs performance and reduces correlations, demonstrating their causal involvement.
In a grid world task, Llama uses temporal difference-like features to predict the actions of a Q-learning agent.
In a graph learning task, Llama learns global graph structure similarly to the successor representation, and temporal difference features support this learning.
papers.limitation:
The sparse autoencoders are task-specific and not suitable for identifying reinforcement learning variables for arbitrary tasks.
A circuit-level understanding of how these representations come about remains unclear.
The alignment between the model's behavior and the Q-learning agent is not perfect.
future_direction: Build more generic sparse autoencoders for arbitrary tasks.
Replicate findings with different large language models.
Achieve a circuit-level understanding of how temporal difference representations are computed.
Extend the Q-learning model to account for repetition tendencies.
papers.abstract: In-context learning, the ability to adapt based on a few examples in the input prompt, is a ubiquitous feature of large language models (LLMs). However, as LLMs' in-context learning abilities continue to improve, understanding this phenomenon mechanistically becomes increasingly important. In particular, it is not well-understood how LLMs learn to solve specific classes of problems, such as reinforcement learning (RL) problems, in-context. Through three different tasks, we first show that Llama $3$ $70$B can solve simple RL problems in-context. We then analyze the residual stream of Llama using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and find representations that closely match temporal difference (TD) errors. Notably, these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token. We verify that these representations are indeed causally involved in the computation of TD errors and $Q$-values by performing carefully designed interventions on them. Taken together, our work establishes a methodology for studying and manipulating in-context learning with SAEs, paving the way for a more mechanistic understanding.

papers.title: SAGE: Scalable Ground Truth Evaluations for Large Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate sparse autoencoders (SAEs) in the absence of ground truth features, and scale such evaluations to large models and tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAGE, a framework that enables scalable ground truth evaluation for sparse autoencoders by automatically discovering task-specific cross-sections and using residual stream SAEs to reduce training overhead.
papers.conclusion: SAGE enables large-scale SAE evaluations on realistic tasks, marking a significant advancement toward generalizable SAE assessments in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE reproduces IOI evaluation results without prior knowledge, using only residual stream SAEs.
SAGE scales to new tasks (induction) and models (Pythia70M, GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2-2).
Larger SAEs (higher dimension) generally perform better in the evaluations.
Supervised feature dictionaries provide high-quality approximations of ground truth features, outperforming unsupervised SAEs in controllability.
The projection-based reconstruction method allows using residual stream SAEs for sublayer activations, reducing training overhead.
papers.limitation: The current approach is constrained by the effectiveness of attribution patching in identifying attribute cross-sections.
future_direction: Expanding task diversity by incorporating tasks with more high-level features and covering larger feature distributions.
Improving discovery methods for attribute cross-sections beyond attribution patching.
Incorporating additional activation disentanglement methods beyond SAEs, such as PCA or Distributed Alignment Search.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in interpretability is to decompose model activations into meaningful features. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for this task. However, a central problem in evaluating the quality of SAEs is the absence of ground truth features to serve as an evaluation gold standard. Current evaluation methods for SAEs are therefore confronted with a significant trade-off: SAEs can either leverage toy models or other proxies with predefined ground truth features; or they use extensive prior knowledge of realistic task circuits. The former limits the generalizability of the evaluation results, while the latter limits the range of models and tasks that can be used for evaluations. We introduce SAGE: Scalable Autoencoder Ground-truth Evaluation, a ground truth evaluation framework for SAEs that scales to large state-of-the-art SAEs and models. We demonstrate that our method can automatically identify task-specific activations and compute ground truth features at these points. Compared to previous methods we reduce the training overhead by introducing a novel reconstruction method that allows to apply residual stream SAEs to sublayer activations. This eliminates the need for SAEs trained on every task-specific activation location. Then we validate the scalability of our framework, by evaluating SAEs on novel tasks on Pythia70M, GPT-2 Small, and Gemma-2-2. Our framework therefore paves the way for generalizable, large-scale evaluations of SAEs in interpretability research.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: One-Step is Enough: Sparse Autoencoders for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders learn interpretable features for text-to-image diffusion models, and do these features generalize across different denoising steps and model architectures?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs can learn interpretable features from one-step text-to-image diffusion models that generalize across steps and architectures, enabling causal intervention and revealing block specialization.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image diffusion models, and one-step training is sufficient for learning features that generalize to multi-step models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on one-step SDXL Turbo generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and multi-step SDXL base model without additional training.
The learned features are interpretable and causally influence the image generation process.
Transformer blocks specialize into roles: up.0.0 for details, up.0.1 for style, and down.2.1 for composition.
RIEBench shows SAE features allow fine-grained image editing with fewer features compared to neuron interventions.
One-step training is sufficient for learning meaningful features applicable to multi-step diffusion models.
papers.limitation: The change pose task is hard to achieve with the current RIEBench setup.
future_direction: Improving feature selection strategies for delete interventions
Extending SAEs to other diffusion models
Using learned features for advanced image editing and control
papers.abstract: For large language models (LLMs), sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been shown to decompose intermediate representations that often are not interpretable directly into sparse sums of interpretable features, facilitating better control and subsequent analysis. However, similar analyses and approaches have been lacking for text-to-image models. We investigate the possibility of using SAEs to learn interpretable features for SDXL Turbo, a few-step text-to-image diffusion model. To this end, we train SAEs on the updates performed by transformer blocks within SDXL Turbo's denoising U-net in its 1-step setting. Interestingly, we find that they generalize to 4-step SDXL Turbo and even to the multi-step SDXL base model (i.e., a different model) without additional training. In addition, we show that their learned features are interpretable, causally influence the generation process, and reveal specialization among the blocks. We do so by creating RIEBench, a representation-based image editing benchmark, for editing images while they are generated by turning on and off individual SAE features. This allows us to track which transformer blocks' features are the most impactful depending on the edit category. Our work is the first investigation of SAEs for interpretability in text-to-image diffusion models and our results establish SAEs as a promising approach for understanding and manipulating the internal mechanisms of text-to-image models.

papers.title: Enhancing Neural Network Interpretability with Feature-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the feature learning of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to better align with input features, thereby enhancing their usefulness for neural network interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Mutual Feature Regularization (MFR), a regularization technique that trains multiple Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) in parallel with weight reinitialization and an auxiliary penalty to encourage learning similar features, leading to better alignment with input features and improved SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: MFR encourages SAEs to learn more features of the input, thereby increasing their usefulness for neural network interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
MFR increases the correlation between feature similarity across SAEs and similarity with input features, as demonstrated on synthetic data.
On synthetic data, SAEs trained with MFR recover more of the known input features compared to baseline SAEs.
MFR improves reconstruction loss and loss recovered when training SAEs on GPT-2 Small MLP layer activations, with up to a 21.21% reduction in reconstruction loss.
MFR also improves reconstruction loss on EEG denoising tasks, though the benefits are smaller than for neural network activations.
The method involves conditionally reinitializing SAE weights based on inactive feature detection and adding an auxiliary penalty to encourage feature similarity across SAEs.
papers.limitation: MFR increases computational cost as it requires training multiple SAEs in parallel, which may become unmanageable for very large models.
future_direction: Investigate efficient mutual learning-based approaches for SAEs that can benefit from the positive relationship between feature similarity across SAEs and feature similarity with input features without requiring more compute.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise in improving the interpretability of neural network activations, but can learn features that are not features of the input, limiting their effectiveness. We propose \textsc{Mutual Feature Regularization} \textbf{(MFR)}, a regularization technique for improving feature learning by encouraging SAEs trained in parallel to learn similar features. We motivate \textsc{MFR} by showing that features learned by multiple SAEs are more likely to correlate with features of the input. By training on synthetic data with known features of the input, we show that \textsc{MFR} can help SAEs learn those features, as we can directly compare the features learned by the SAE with the input features for the synthetic data. We then scale \textsc{MFR} to SAEs that are trained to denoise electroencephalography (EEG) data and SAEs that are trained to reconstruct GPT-2 Small activations. We show that \textsc{MFR} can improve the reconstruction loss of SAEs by up to 21.21\% on GPT-2 Small, and 6.67\% on EEG data. Our results suggest that the similarity between features learned by different SAEs can be leveraged to improve SAE training, thereby enhancing performance and the usefulness of SAEs for model interpretability.

papers.title: Features Emerge as Discrete States: The First Application of SAEs to 3D Representations
papers.research_question: How do features in a 3D reconstruction model behave, and what learning dynamics explain their discrete state-like nature?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first application of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to 3D data, analyzing a 3D reconstruction VAE. It finds that the model encodes features as discrete states rather than continuous ones and provides a theoretical framework based on learning dynamics to explain this behavior and other observed phenomena like the bimodal distribution of transition points.
papers.conclusion: The work successfully applies SAEs to 3D data, revealing discrete feature representations and providing a framework of feature learning dynamics that explains the observed discretization and the counter-intuitive bimodality of transition points through a proposed mechanism of superposition interference redistribution.
papers.key_findings:
Features in the 3D reconstruction model Dora-VAE are discrete and state-like, approximating a discrete state space driven by phase-like transitions.
High-impact features have transition points that form a unimodal distribution centered around t≈0.5.
Low-impact features have transition points that form a symmetric bimodal distribution when aggregated across all features.
The model appears to redistribute interference from superposition to prioritize high-impact features, shifting the transition points of low-impact features.
Feature ablation and addition experiments demonstrate the causal relationship between specific features and the reconstructed 3D shape's position and structure.
papers.limitation: The findings are based on a single model (Dora-VAE) applied to 3D data and may not generalize to other models or domains.
future_direction: Validating observations across other domains (text, image) and models (PointNet++, LION).
Examining Dora-VAE with circuit detection techniques to see how features flow through the architecture.
Probing gradients of toy models to evaluate the proposed feature learning framework.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a powerful dictionary learning technique for decomposing neural network activations, translating the hidden state into human ideas with high semantic value despite no external intervention or guidance. However, this technique has rarely been applied outside of the textual domain, limiting theoretical explorations of feature decomposition. We present the first application of SAEs to the 3D domain, analyzing the features used by a state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction VAE applied to 53k 3D models from the Objaverse dataset. We observe that the network encodes discrete rather than continuous features, leading to our key finding: such models approximate a discrete state space, driven by phase-like transitions from feature activations. Through this state transition framework, we address three otherwise unintuitive behaviors - the inclination of the reconstruction model towards positional encoding representations, the sigmoidal behavior of reconstruction loss from feature ablation, and the bimodality in the distribution of phase transition points. This final observation suggests the model redistributes the interference caused by superposition to prioritize the saliency of different features. Our work not only compiles and explains unexpected phenomena regarding feature decomposition, but also provides a framework to explain the model's feature learning dynamics. The code and dataset of encoded 3D objects will be available on release.

papers.title: Group Equivariance Meets Mechanistic Interpretability: Equivariant Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can group symmetries be incorporated into sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, and does this lead to more useful features in downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adaptively equivariant sparse autoencoders that incorporate group symmetries, which learn features leading to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Adding domain-specific properties like group equivariance to sparse autoencoders can significantly increase their utility in domains beyond language, despite being early results.
papers.key_findings:
A single matrix M can explain more than 98% of the variance in how neural network activations transform under input transformations by a discrete cyclic group.
Equivariant SAEs learn more informative directions in activation space, leading to increased performance on group-structured probing tasks.
Equivariant SAEs lag behind regular SAEs in the reconstruction/sparsity frontier.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to a synthetic task, relatively small models, and a small discrete group.
future_direction: Can M be learned as effectively in larger models such as frontier foundation models?
Can the optimization of M be improved by better utilizing the group structure, e.g., by constraining the optimization to M^|G| = I?
Does the two-layer encoder qualitatively alter what kind of features are discovered, and how can the features best be labeled incorporating the knowledge of how they transform with M?
Can the reconstruction performance of the equivariant SAE be improved to match that of regular SAEs?
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven useful in disentangling the opaque activations of neural networks, primarily large language models, into sets of interpretable features. However, adapting them to domains beyond language, such as scientific data with group symmetries, introduces challenges that can hinder their effectiveness. We show that incorporating such group symmetries into the SAEs yields features more useful in downstream tasks. More specifically, we train autoencoders on synthetic images and find that a single matrix can explain how their activations transform as the images are rotated. Building on this, we develop adaptively equivariant SAEs that can adapt to the base model's level of equivariance. These adaptive SAEs discover features that lead to superior probing performance compared to regular SAEs, demonstrating the value of incorporating symmetries in mechanistic interpretability tools.

papers.title: Data Whitening Improves Sparse Autoencoder Learning
papers.research_question: Does applying PCA whitening to input activations improve the interpretability of features learned by sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: PCA whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) at a slight cost to reconstruction fidelity, by transforming the optimization landscape to be more convex and isotropic.
papers.conclusion: PCA whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, especially when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.
papers.key_findings:
Whitening transforms the SAE optimization landscape, making it more convex and isotropic, which improves feature recovery.
Whitening significantly improves interpretability metrics (sparse probing, SCR, TPP) for ReLU SAEs.
Whitening improves sparse probing for Top-K SAEs but does not significantly affect SCR or TPP.
Whitening causes a small but significant decrease in reconstruction quality (CE Loss and explained variance).
The benefits of whitening are more pronounced for ReLU-based SAEs than for Top-K SAEs.
papers.limitation: Experiments focus on middle layers of language models at the sub-2B parameter scale.
future_direction: Explore whitening's effects across different layers (early vs. late).
Investigate whitening on larger model scales (>2B parameters) and other architectures/modalities (vision, audio).
Study interactions between whitening and other training innovations (e.g., gated SAEs, transcoders).
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for learning interpretable features from neural network activations. However, the optimization landscape for SAE training can be challenging due to correlations in the input data. We demonstrate that applying PCA Whitening to input activations -- a standard preprocessing technique in classical sparse coding -- improves SAE performance across multiple metrics. Through theoretical analysis and simulation, we show that whitening transforms the optimization landscape, making it more convex and easier to navigate. We evaluate both ReLU and Top-K SAEs across diverse model architectures, widths, and sparsity regimes. Empirical evaluation on SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark for sparse autoencoders, reveals that whitening consistently improves interpretability metrics, including sparse probing accuracy and feature disentanglement, despite minor drops in reconstruction quality. Our results challenge the assumption that interpretability aligns with an optimal sparsity--fidelity trade-off and suggest that whitening should be considered as a default preprocessing step for SAE training, particularly when interpretability is prioritized over perfect reconstruction.

papers.title: Gemma Scope: Open Sparse Autoencoders Everywhere All At Once on Gemma 2
papers.research_question: How can we make sparse autoencoder research more accessible by providing a comprehensive open suite of SAEs trained on Gemma 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Gemma Scope, a comprehensive open suite of sparse autoencoders trained on Gemma 2 models, to accelerate interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Gemma Scope provides a valuable resource for the interpretability community and hopes it will enable and accelerate downstream research.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs show a sparsity-fidelity trade-off, with wider SAEs providing better fidelity at a given sparsity.
SAEs trained on base models transfer reasonably well to instruction-tuned models, with only a small increase in loss.
Reconstruction loss varies with token position, increasing rapidly for the first few tokens.
SAEs perform better on mathematical data and worse on multilingual data.
Using bfloat16 for inference has negligible impact on SAE performance.
papers.limitation: There is no consensus on reliable metrics for evaluating sparse autoencoder quality.
future_direction: Improving SAEs to capture circular features efficiently.
Using SAEs to improve interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
Investigating how SAEs can be used for circuit analysis in larger models.
papers.abstract: Tom Lieberum, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, Lewis Smith, Nicolas Sonnerat, Vikrant Varma, Janos Kramar, Anca Dragan, Rohin Shah, Neel Nanda. Proceedings of the 7th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP. 2024.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Sparsification and Reconstruction from the Perspective of Representation Geometry
papers.research_question: How does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vectors from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance?
papers.core_contribution: This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance, emphasizing the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for improving SAEs and developing novel tools for decomposing neural networks from the perspective of representation geometry, particularly emphasizing the necessity of understanding and incorporating representation geometry constraints.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit stratified manifolds where representations of the same concept are distributed across different manifolds.
Sparse encoding reduces feature overlap by merging similar semantic features within local representations and introducing more dimensionality, achieving feature disentanglement.
Increased separability between different local representations causally enhances reconstruction performance in SAEs.
The variability of the feature modal rank (r3) and AGD under noise validates the stratified structure of representations.
Global representations are compressed during sparse encoding, while local representations gain effective dimensionality and connected components.
papers.limitation:
Extraction of activations depends on prompts related to the concept, not guaranteeing all representations are captured.
Regularization in SAEs is not included as a controlled variable, and differences in representation structure caused by variations in regularization require further exploration.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a predominant tool in mechanistic interpretability, aiming to identify interpretable monosemantic features. However, how does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vector from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance? To address these questions, we propose the SAEMA, which validates the stratified structure of the representation by observing the variability of the rank of the symmetric semipositive definite (SSPD) matrix corresponding to the modal tensor unfolded along the latent tensor with the level of noise added to the residual stream. To systematically investigate how sparse encoding alters representational structures, we define local and global representations, demonstrating that they amplify inter-feature distinctions by merging similar semantic features and introducing additional dimensionality. Furthermore, we intervene the global representation from an optimization perspective, proving a significant causal relationship between their separability and the reconstruction performance. This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance. Particularly emphasizes the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints, providing empirical references for developing new interpretable tools and improving SAEs. The code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}.

papers.title: Training Superior Sparse Autoencoders for Instruct Models
papers.research_question: How can we effectively train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on instruct models, given that existing methods designed for base models result in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Finetuning-aligned Sequential Training (FAST), a novel method for training sparse autoencoders on instruct models that aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns of instruct models, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction quality and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FAST is an effective method for training SAEs on instruct models, achieving superior reconstruction and feature interpretability, and the resulting SAEs can be used to steer model behavior via special token features, opening new avenues for model control.
papers.key_findings:
FAST significantly outperforms baseline Block Training methods (BT(P) and BT(F)) in token reconstruction (MSE) and special token reconstruction (MSEst) across multiple instruct models and SAE architectures.
FAST produces a higher proportion of high-quality, interpretable features compared to baseline methods, as measured by an automated feature interpretability scoring framework.
Intervening on the activations of special tokens via the trained SAEs can improve output quality and enable fine-grained control of model behavior, suggesting new applications for SAEs.
future_direction: Exploring the opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior through steering with SAE latents, particularly via special tokens.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow in scale and capability, understanding their internal mechanisms becomes increasingly critical. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a key tool in mechanistic interpretability, enabling the extraction of human-interpretable features from LLMs. However, existing SAE training methods are primarily designed for base models, resulting in reduced reconstruction quality and interpretability when applied to instruct models. To bridge this gap, we propose $\underline{\textbf{F}}$inetuning-$\underline{\textbf{a}}$ligned $\underline{\textbf{S}}$equential $\underline{\textbf{T}}$raining ($\textit{FAST}$), a novel training method specifically tailored for instruct models. $\textit{FAST}$ aligns the training process with the data distribution and activation patterns characteristic of instruct models, resulting in substantial improvements in both reconstruction and feature interpretability. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $\textit{FAST}$ achieves a mean squared error of 0.6468 in token reconstruction, significantly outperforming baseline methods with errors of 5.1985 and 1.5096. In feature interpretability, $\textit{FAST}$ yields a higher proportion of high-quality features, for Llama3.2-3B-Instruct, $21.1\%$ scored in the top range, compared to $7.0\%$ and $10.2\%$ for $\textit{BT(P)}$ and $\textit{BT(F)}$. Surprisingly, we discover that intervening on the activations of special tokens via the SAEs leads to improvements in output quality, suggesting new opportunities for fine-grained control of model behavior. Code, data, and 240 trained SAEs are available at https://github.com/Geaming2002/FAST.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders on Targeted Concept Erasure Tasks
papers.research_question: How can we develop effective evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) that measure their ability to disentangle concepts and remove spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces two evaluation metrics for Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs): an automated version of SHIFT and the novel Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric, which measure SAEs' ability to disentangle and causally isolate concepts.
papers.conclusion: SHIFT and TPP are effective, computationally efficient metrics for evaluating SAEs that can be applied to a wide range of datasets and show improvement during training, but they should be used as part of a broader evaluation suite due to their limitations.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT and TPP effectively differentiate between SAE architectures, with TopK and JumpReLU outperforming Standard SAEs.
Both metrics show improvement throughout SAE training, with most gains in the first 10% of training.
The metrics can be computed efficiently without an LLM judge, but using an LLM judge increases confidence and correlates well with the unfiltered versions.
The optimal sparsity for each metric differs, indicating a trade-off between sparsity and performance.
A single TopK SAE can achieve better performance on SHIFT than multiple Standard SAEs, as shown in the Pythia-70M experiments.
papers.limitation:
The LLM judge has a lower bar for interpretability than standard automated interpretability methods, potentially leading to false negatives.
The evaluation metrics rely on subjective hypotheses about human-understandable concepts, which may not reflect the model's true internal representations.
Hyperparameter selection and SAE latent selection are challenging due to lack of ground truth and variability across model sizes.
The metrics focus on causal isolation of concepts, but high-quality SAEs should also exhibit other characteristics like sparsity and disentanglement.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are an interpretability technique aimed at decomposing neural network activations into interpretable units. However, a major bottleneck for SAE development has been the lack of high-quality performance metrics, with prior work largely relying on unsupervised proxies. In this work, we introduce a family of evaluations based on SHIFT, a downstream task from Marks et al. (Sparse Feature Circuits, 2024) in which spurious cues are removed from a classifier by ablating SAE features judged to be task-irrelevant by a human annotator. We adapt SHIFT into an automated metric of SAE quality; this involves replacing the human annotator with an LLM. Additionally, we introduce the Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) metric that quantifies an SAE's ability to disentangle similar concepts, effectively scaling SHIFT to a wider range of datasets. We apply both SHIFT and TPP to multiple open-source models, demonstrating that these metrics effectively differentiate between various SAE training hyperparameters and architectures.

papers.title: Towards scientific discovery with dictionary learning: Extracting biological concepts from microscopy foundation models
papers.research_question: Can dictionary learning extract meaningful high-level concepts from unsupervised vision foundation models trained on scientific data (cell microscopy images) where prior knowledge about concepts is limited?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ICFL, a novel sparse dictionary learning algorithm combined with PCA whitening, to successfully extract biologically meaningful concepts (e.g., cell types, genetic perturbations) from frozen representations of vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning, specifically ICFL with PCA whitening, is a powerful and promising approach for extracting interpretable biological concepts from microscopy foundation models, enabling new directions for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
ICFL combined with PCA whitening extracts sparse features that correlate with biological concepts such as cell types and genetic perturbations.
ICFL reduces the number of 'dead features' compared to TopK SAEs.
Linear probes on reconstructions from ICFL features preserve significant biological information, with accuracies comparable to probes on original representations.
ICFL features achieve selectivity scores comparable to handcrafted CellProfiler features for identifying genetic perturbations.
Token-level heatmaps from feature directions enable interpretation of subtle morphological changes, such as distinguishing perturbed from control-like cells.
future_direction: Assess whether peak selectivity of handcrafted features can be matched using deep learning-based approaches with fewer non-zero elements.
Future research on interpreting and validating concept directions found in large foundation models for microscopy image data.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (DL) has emerged as a powerful approach to extract semantically meaningful concepts from the internals of large language models (LLMs) trained mainly in the text domain. In this work, we explore whether DL can extract meaningful concepts from less human-interpretable scientific data, such as vision foundation models trained on cell microscopy images, where limited prior knowledge exists about which high-level concepts should arise. We propose a novel combination of a sparse DL algorithm, Iterative Codebook Feature Learning (ICFL), with a PCA whitening pre-processing step derived from control data. Using this combined approach, we successfully retrieve biologically meaningful concepts, such as cell types and genetic perturbations. Moreover, we demonstrate how our method reveals subtle morphological changes arising from human-interpretable interventions, offering a promising new direction for scientific discovery via mechanistic interpretability in bioimaging.

papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do various representation-based steering methods compare to prompting and finetuning in terms of concept detection and model steering for language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AXBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating steering and concept detection methods, and finds that prompting outperforms representation-based methods for steering, while difference-in-means and probes are best for detection, with the novel ReFT-r1 method being competitive on both tasks.
papers.conclusion: Representation steering methods largely lag behind prompting and finetuning, but ReFT-r1 shows that steering can be improved with comprehensive benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting is the best method for model steering, outperforming all representation-based methods.
Difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 perform best for concept detection with no significant difference between them.
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are not competitive compared to other methods on both steering and detection.
ReFT-r1, a novel weakly-supervised method, is competitive on both steering and detection tasks while offering interpretability advantages.
The AXBENCH benchmark enables comprehensive evaluation and comparison of steering methods.
papers.limitation: Hyperparameter tuning might underestimate steering performance due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Extend AXBENCH to arbitrary concept descriptions and add new evaluation tasks as better feature-labelling techniques and steering approaches emerge.
papers.abstract: Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals, but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs), linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning; ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning for language models? The paper proposes using board game models with known interpretable features as a testbed to evaluate sparse autoencoder quality.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces board game models as a testbed for evaluating sparse autoencoders, proposes two new metrics (coverage and board reconstruction) for SAE quality, and introduces p-annealing, a training technique that improves SAE performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a more objective paradigm for evaluating SAE quality with coverage and board reconstruction metrics, and shows that p-annealing improves SAE training.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features can accurately reconstruct game boards, though they do not match linear probe performance.
Standard SAEs trained with p-annealing perform on par with Gated SAEs on existing metrics and show improvement on the new metrics.
Coverage and board reconstruction metrics reveal differences in SAE quality not captured by unsupervised metrics like L0 and loss recovered.
The metrics are optimal in the elbow region of the Pareto frontier, validating common wisdom about SAE quality.
papers.limitation:
The metrics are confined to chess and Othello domains, raising concerns about generalizability.
The set of board state properties is determined by researchers based on domain knowledge, potentially overlooking essential features.
The evaluation does not directly address how learned features could be used for downstream interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: What latent features are encoded in language model (LM) representations? Recent work on training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to disentangle interpretable features in LM representations has shown significant promise. However, evaluating the quality of these SAEs is difficult because we lack a ground-truth collection of interpretable features that we expect good SAEs to recover. We thus propose to measure progress in interpretable dictionary learning by working in the setting of LMs trained on chess and Othello transcripts. These settings carry natural collections of interpretable features -- for example, "there is a knight on F3" -- which we leverage into $\textit{supervised}$ metrics for SAE quality. To guide progress in interpretable dictionary learning, we introduce a new SAE training technique, $\textit{p-annealing}$, which improves performance on prior unsupervised metrics as well as our new metrics.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Interpreting CLIP with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve sparse autoencoders to better interpret vision-language models like CLIP by achieving a better trade-off between reconstruction quality and sparsity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoder (MSAE), a hierarchical SAE architecture that achieves state-of-the-art Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality and sparsity for CLIP, enabling effective interpretation and control via concept extraction.
papers.conclusion: MSAE provides an effective method for interpreting and controlling CLIP through hierarchical sparse autoencoding, with practical applications in concept-based similarity search and bias analysis.
papers.key_findings:
MSAE establishes a new Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality (0.99 cosine similarity, <0.1 FVU) and sparsity (~80%) for CLIP.
MSAE extracts over 120 interpretable semantic concepts from CLIP's representation space, validated across image and text modalities.
MSAE enables concept-based similarity search and bias analysis, demonstrated on downstream tasks like CelebA for gender bias.
papers.limitation: The concept mapping approach has limitations, including potential poor assignments when no good matches exist and challenges with hierarchical concepts due to non-orthogonal semantic feature vectors or incomplete vocabulary coverage.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are useful for detecting and steering interpretable features in neural networks, with particular potential for understanding complex multimodal representations. Given their ability to uncover interpretable features, SAEs are particularly valuable for analyzing large-scale vision-language models (e.g., CLIP and SigLIP), which are fundamental building blocks in modern systems yet remain challenging to interpret and control. However, current SAE methods are limited by optimizing both reconstruction quality and sparsity simultaneously, as they rely on either activation suppression or rigid sparsity constraints. To this end, we introduce Matryoshka SAE (MSAE), a new architecture that learns hierarchical representations at multiple granularities simultaneously, enabling a direct optimization of both metrics without compromise. MSAE establishes a new state-of-the-art Pareto frontier between reconstruction quality and sparsity for CLIP, achieving 0.99 cosine similarity and less than 0.1 fraction of variance unexplained while maintaining ~80% sparsity. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of MSAE as a tool for interpreting and controlling CLIP by extracting over 120 semantic concepts from its representation to perform concept-based similarity search and bias analysis in downstream tasks like CelebA. We make the codebase available at https://github.com/WolodjaZ/MSAE.

papers.title: Neurogenesis-Inspired Dictionary Learning: Online Model Adaption in a Changing World
papers.research_question: How can online dictionary learning be adapted to non-stationary data streams by dynamically adding and removing dictionary elements?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a neurogenesis-inspired online dictionary learning algorithm that dynamically adapts the dictionary size and structure via addition and removal of dictionary elements, outperforming fixed-size online dictionary learning in non-stationary environments.
papers.conclusion: Neurogenesis-inspired dictionary learning is effective for online adaptation in non-stationary environments, and conditions for its superiority are identified.
papers.key_findings:
NODL outperforms fixed-size ODL in non-stationary environments, especially with sparse dictionaries.
The interplay between birth and death of dictionary elements leads to better adaptation and memory retention.
Sparse dictionaries yield better classification performance than dense dictionaries.
NODL is robust to parameter variations.
Theoretical analysis shows ODL cannot adapt to new domains with non-overlapping support in sparse data.
future_direction: extending to deep and nonlinear autoencoders
extending to supervised setting
papers.abstract: We address the problem of online model adaptation when learning representations from non-stationary data streams. Specifically, we focus here on online dictionary learning (i.e. sparse linear autoencoder), and propose a simple but effective online model selection approach involving “birth” (addition) and “death” (removal) of hidden units representing dictionary elements, in response to changing inputs; we draw inspiration from the adult neurogenesis phenomenon in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus, known to be associated with better adaptation to new environments. Empirical evaluation on real-life datasets (images and text), as well as on synthetic data, demonstrates that the proposed approach can considerably outperform the state-of-art non-adaptive online sparse coding of [Mairal et al., 2009] in the presence of non-stationary data. Moreover, we identify certain data- and model properties associated with such improvements.

papers.title: MedSAE: Dissecting MedCLIP Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to improve interpretability of medical vision-language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Medical Sparse Autoencoders (MedSAEs) to extract interpretable, monosemantic features from MedCLIP embeddings, advancing mechanistic interpretability in medical vision.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a first step toward mechanistic interpretability in medical vision-language models, highlighting sparse autoencoders as a promising direction for building transparent, robust, and trustworthy medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
MedSAE neurons achieve lower entropy (2.25) than raw MedCLIP features (2.38), indicating higher monosemanticity.
21 medically meaningful features are identified with MedGEMMA-based automated naming, with detection accuracy above 70%.
MedSAE features show stronger alignment with clinical concepts compared to raw embeddings.
papers.limitation:
presence of inactive neurons and the need for more expressive SAE architectures
computational cost and dataset sensitivity of automated naming
limited validation across modalities and institutions
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence in healthcare requires models that are accurate and interpretable.
